newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine judge charges US drags feet in IBM case.
newsitem.headline: Argentine judge charges US drags feet in IBM case.

text.p: An Argentine judge probing an alleged bribery case involving International Business Machines Corp's local unit Tuesday charged that U.S. courts are reluctant to hand him bank account information he requested more than a year ago.

Judge Adolfo Bagnasco told Reuters he sent the Argentine government a document for delivery to U.S. authorities demanding to know why, "notwithstanding the long time passed, no information has been delivered to this court."
"This can clearly be considered a reluctant attitude from the requested (U.S.) authorities," the document said.

Bagnasco is investigating whether bribes were paid in 1993 to ensure that U.S. computer giant International Business Machines Corp won a $250 million deal to install a computer system in state-run Banco Nacin.
Eleven people, including former Banco Nacin head Aldo Dadone and IBM Argentina's ex-President Ricardo Martorana and former Vice-President Gustavo Soriani, have been indicted in the case.
At the heart of the probe are payments made to IBM's subcontractor CCR, which the judge suspects may have gone to alleged bribes for IBM Argentina to win the contract.
Bagnasco has asked U.S. authorities to hand him information on a Citicorp account in New York where money from CCR was transferred and is probing other banks' accounts.
He traced CCR's deposits for about $9 million in an account of a Banque Bruxelles Lambert SA bank branch in Geneva, and at his request the Swiss supreme court lifted banking secrecy in August.
"Swiss courts have acted much more quickly in spite of their difficulties," Bagnasco said, pointing out that, unlike the United States, Switzerland has bank secrecy rules.
IBM Argentina has so far denied any wrongdoing although it has admitted to errors "inconsistent with company policy."

Banco Nacin this year cancelled the deal and sued IBM Argentina for $174 million, accusing it in a Buenos Aires Administrative Contentious Court, which arbitrates commercial disputes, of not complying with deadlines. IBM countersued for $86 million, alleging "wrongful revocation" of the contract.
Other IBM Argentina deals are under separate probes.

A separate judge is probing alleged "serious irregularities" in the $425 million cost and awarding by decree of a deal between the firm and the country's tax collection body, DGI. Another is probing why a deal between the company and the province of Mendoza government was awarded by decree instead of by tender.
